contradicted: The dispatch's premise was contradicted by the repo, and it is stated here rather than quietly built around. (1) 'The writer: src/parcel-node/reconcile-county-parcel-nodes.ts ... no share, threshold or authorisation appears in it' is TRUE of that file and was read by the dispatch as meaning this writer has no blast-radius refusal at all. What was actually missing is what P-328's plan row says: the engine read its OWN number (0.05) and its OWN env var name, with no drift check against the program's, and a second writer in the same class was named in P-213's header and not fixed. (2) The dispatch warns that 'a second copy of a constant is a number that can drift' -- and taking the factory's 0.5 means the engine now CARRIES a copy, so the copy is pinned to the factory file's bytes with the drift check that makes it fire. (3) CP1 itself declared an edit that was not made and did not need to be: the measured destructive pair is already on the plan reconcileCountyParcelNodes returns (priorActive, orphans) -- they are literally the two numbers the guard call passes -- so no edit was made to a file covered by a pinned test, and the declined edit is stated in CP2 rather than narrated as done. leave_behind: OPERATOR DECISION (the row's own open question, unchanged from CP1): the program's single number is 0.5 and this lane implements it, which WEAKENS the engine's live control on the writer that produced the incident -- 0.05 -> 0.5 is a 10x loosening on the parcel-node and reactivation shares, and a run retiring 40 percent of a county (a mass false retirement the old number refused) now passes without authorisation. Bastrop's 92.5 percent is refused either way, so the row's predicate holds; the loss is in the band between 5 and 50 percent. If the operator prefers the sharper number, it changes in ONE place (the factory's declaration) and both repos follow via the drift check. Nothing in this lane should be read as having measured the right value for that number.

FACTORY ROW (the enforceable cross-repo direction, and the one this lane cannot close): hauska-engine is public and hauska-factory is private, so the factory can read the public engine's declaration in its CI and the engine can never read the factory's. The pattern already exists (P-331: each repo's CI reads the other's main). Until a factory-side check reads packages/engine-core/scripts/destructive-write-declaration.mjs and fails on disagreement, a change to the factory's 0.5 is caught on the engine side only when someone runs the re-derivation leg with a local clone -- which CI does not have and must not need.

ENGINE ROW: the producers are pure and the refusal is a call-site convention. Closing it properly means the guard's return shape carries an unforgeable authorisation that a write path cannot be constructed without -- a type-system change, not this row. Until then the register scan is the detector for the shape, and the limit is stated in three places rather than implied.

ENGINE ROW: the two registers (engine DESTRUCTIVE_WRITERS, factory DESTRUCTIVE_WRITERS) are not joined. A reader of either cannot see the other, and a writer that exists in both repos is enumerated twice with no link. The factory-side row above is the cheapest way to join them; a shared published list would be the other, and it would need a home in the public repo to be readable by both.

ENGINE ROW (small): the building-footprint absence DELETE is genuinely set-valued and county-scoped, and it is NOT wired because its normal share is near 1.0 by design. That judgement is written in the register, and it is the entry most likely to be wrong: if a future change makes a normal footprint acquisition delete only a small share, the guard would be right to fire and nothing would notice it is not wired. Re-read that entry before changing the footprint writer.

The threshold 0.5 is a DECLARATION with its basis in the factory's own header, not a measurement of a series. The engine now records it in one place with a drift check; neither repo has a series that would tell anyone whether 0.5 is right.

FACTORY ROW: make hauska-factory's CI read the public engine's declaration and fail on disagreement -- the only enforceable cross-repo direction (see leave_behind).

fleetMemory.LESSON: A PIN IS ONLY A PIN IF SOMETHING READS EVERY FIELD IT RECORDS. The declaration's pin recorded the factory file's byte length, git blob sha and a normalized sha256, and its own refusal-code facts -- and the first version of the drift check compared none of them: it compared the engine's constant to the pin's constant and stopped. Every recorded-but-unread field is drift that LOOKS checked, which is the P-320 defect ('a second copy is a number that can drift') reproduced one layer down, inside the control built to fix it.
